sentences.text: The holotype specimen includes parts of the skull, jaw, vertebrae, limbs, and armor plates, indicating the animal was likely covered in body armor made of osteoderms.

Estimates for the juvenile holotype suggest it was 2 to 2.5 meters long and weighed between 50 and 90 kilograms, whereas adults are estimated to have reached lengths of 3 to 4 meters and weights up to 240 kilograms.
Fossils of Emausaurus were found in the Lehmhagen Member in northern Germany, specifically in Bituminous Shale in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
The species Emausaurus ernsti was named and described by Hartmut Haubold in 1990, though later sources note the formal description occurred in 1991.
Emausaurus was likely a low-browsing herbivore that ate cycads and Bennettitales.
Emausaurus possessed a sinuous jaw profile, a feature more advanced than that of the basal genus Scutellosaurus.

Emausaurus forelimbs were adapted for weight support rather than grasping, with conical, slightly curved claws, suggesting it was a quadrupedal, low-roaming herbivore adapted for supporting its weight.

Cladistic analyses place Emausaurus as a basal member of the Thyreophora, between Scutellosaurus and Scelidosaurus, showing it was more derived than Scutellosaurus but less derived than Scelidosaurus.
Its parent group is Scelidosauridae, and it belongs to the family Scelidosauridae.
It is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Emausaurus lived approximately 185 million years ago during the Early Jurassic Toarcian, specifically between 184.2 and 182.9 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
The holotype was found in a Lower Toarcian shale layer at the Emausaurus type site.

The fossil site contains invertebrates including insects, bivalves, sea snails, and ammonites, alongside fish fossils from the site that include the genera Saurorhynchus, Grimmenichthys, and Grimmenodon.
The phylogenetic position of Emausaurus is controversial because the known specimen is immature.
Researchers have debated whether Emausaurus is more derived than Scelidosaurus or a sister taxon to Stegosauria.
Later studies criticize assumptions of bipedality or quadrupedality in Emausaurus due to its incomplete nature and close relationship with Scutellosaurus.
